title: How reliable is a weather forecast for a calendar event?
short: Read forecast uncertainty before changing a plan
description: Check forecast place, period and uncertainty before changing an event. Separate rain probability, decisions and available weather in Cloud Calendars.
lede: A forecast helps you make a decision about an event; it does not guarantee the conditions at every moment. Start with the venue and time, then decide what information could change the plan. This guide is published by Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars.
commonBelief: A weather icon promises the exact conditions throughout an appointment, and a changed forecast means the earlier probability was meaningless.

sections.heading: Identify the forecast before judging it
body: A useful check starts with the place, date and period being forecast. The same icon beside a daily summary and an hourly entry does not describe the same interval. Read the accompanying values and the provider’s definitions rather than treating the picture as a minute-by-minute promise.

For an outdoor appointment, write down the venue and the hours that matter: arrival, the activity and departure may need different checks. A forecast for your current location does not answer a question about a venue elsewhere.

sections.heading: Understand why an estimate can change
body: The Met Office explains that forecasts start from an estimated state of the atmosphere. Small differences in that starting estimate can grow. Its ensemble systems explore possible outcomes with multiple runs; greater disagreement signals greater uncertainty.

This explains why confidence matters, but does not mean every value in Cloud Calendars is an ensemble mean or that the app displays individual model runs. An icon alone does not reveal the complete uncertainty behind a forecast.

sections.heading: Keep probability, amount and timing separate
body: A rain probability concerns a defined event over a defined place and period. It is not, by itself, a statement about the share of your appointment that will be wet. Check the forecast product’s definitions and read amount, wind or other relevant fields separately when available.

If a forecast changes from rain around midday to rain later, compare the same location and intervals before calling the two versions contradictory. Save the observation time if you need to discuss the change with a venue or another organiser; do not silently move a shared booking.

sections.heading: Choose the decision for the activity
body: The Met Office’s decision-making guidance relates probability thresholds to the particular application. A percentage that prompts one action is not a universal cancellation rule.

For a casual picnic, a nearby indoor alternative may be practical. A booked performance may instead require a venue decision and a notification deadline. Agree who can change the plan, what information they need and when others will hear. These are planning examples, not weather safety thresholds.

sections.heading: Use Cloud Calendars for the schedule and available weather
body: Check that you are looking at the intended day and weather location. Read the forecast only for periods actually supplied; a calendar appointment can exist beyond the available forecast horizon. Missing weather is not a forecast of clear conditions.

If you create an event from a weather hour, review its start, end, destination calendar and location before saving. In the current source this flow proposes a one-hour event and the default new-event calendar. Those draft values are conveniences, not a reservation or a complete travel plan.

sections.heading: Recheck with a purpose and communicate the result
body: Choose a review time that still leaves room to act under your booking’s conditions. At that point, compare the latest relevant forecast with the plan and any applicable official or venue guidance. Repeated refreshing without an available decision does not create certainty.

If the plan changes, edit the correct event or recurrence scope and check the saved result. Confirm important changes directly with the people involved. A calendar alert, a changed forecast and a message received by a participant are three different outcomes.

practical: Check the venue, date, time zone and the forecast period.
Read probability separately from amount, timing and other available weather fields.
Use the provider’s definitions; do not infer confidence from an icon alone.
Agree the fallback, decision owner and deadline for your actual activity.
Review the event’s calendar, start, end and location before saving a change.
Recheck at the agreed time and confirm important changes with participants.

faq.q: Does a rain percentage tell me how long my event will be wet?
faq.a: No. Read what event, place and period the provider defines. A percentage alone does not supply the duration, amount or the conditions at every moment.

faq.q: Does Cloud Calendars show all ensemble model runs?
faq.a: This guide does not claim an ensemble comparison interface. Use the weather values actually available for the selected place and period; do not infer hidden model confidence from an icon.

faq.q: Can I use weather for every future calendar appointment?
faq.a: A calendar can hold dates beyond the available forecast horizon. Check whether the relevant period has weather data and arrange a later review when it does not.
